summary: Serbia is a landlocked country in the central Balkan Peninsula that was once the core of Yugoslavia; its capital, Belgrade, lies at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In the 9th century the Serbs accepted Christianity under Byzantine influence, and in 1219 Saint Sava won autocephaly for the Serbian church, founding the independent Serbian Orthodox Church. After the Ottoman Empire conquered Serbia in the 15th century, the Patriarchate of Peć, restored in 1557, preserved the language, the veneration of saints and national memory through some four hundred years of rule, and Orthodoxy thus became closely bound to Serbian national identity. Religion was suppressed in the communist era, but after the breakup of Yugoslavia and the intensification of ethnic conflict in the 1990s, Orthodoxy became a symbol of Serb identity, and the share of believers rose back above 80 percent.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholics are mainly the Hungarians, Croats and Bunjevci of the northern province of Vojvodina. Before 1918 Vojvodina belonged for a long time to the Catholic Kingdom of Hungary and the Habsburg Empire, and its inhabitants continued the Central European Catholic tradition, so Catholicism is concentrated in northern towns such as Subotica and is only a minority faith nationwide.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived after the Ottoman conquest in the 15th century, when some Slavs and Albanians converted to gain tax and social advantages. After Serbia became independent in the 19th century, many Muslims moved to Ottoman territory; the communities that remained are mainly the Bosniaks of the southwestern Sandžak region (around Novi Pazar) and the Albanians of the Preševo Valley in the south.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The Yugoslav communist government (1945–1991) pursued secularization and weakened the position of the church, but during the civil wars of the 1990s religion and national identity became tied together again, and many people regarded themselves as Orthodox even if they rarely went to church. As a result, very few people clearly stated that they had no religion in the 2022 census, and they were concentrated among the younger generation in large cities such as Belgrade.

religion.background: The Serbs converted to Christianity under Byzantine influence in the 9th century, and in 1219 Saint Sava established the autocephalous Serbian church; during the Middle Ages the Nemanjić dynasty built a great many monasteries. From 1459 the Ottoman Empire ruled for nearly four hundred years and brought Islam, while the Orthodox Church became the core institution preserving Serb culture. Northern Vojvodina was under Habsburg rule, so Catholic and Protestant communities are concentrated there. Secularization was pursued in communist Yugoslavia, and after the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s religion and ethnic identity became closely bound together again.

language.official: Serbian is the official language, and Vojvodina additionally has several minority official languages.

ranking.name: Serbian
ranking.description: Serbian belongs to the South Slavic branch and is the mother tongue of the Serbs. In the 19th century the linguist Vuk Karadžić reformed the Cyrillic alphabet on the principle of "write as you speak," and in 1850 he and Croatian scholars signed the Vienna Literary Agreement, laying the foundation of a common standard language. In the Yugoslav period it was referred to together with Croatian as Serbo-Croatian, and after the state's breakup each was named separately; Serbs make up more than 80 percent of the population, so Serbian is the mother tongue of the vast majority, and both the Cyrillic and Latin alphabets are used.

ranking.name: Hungarian
ranking.description: Hungarian speakers are concentrated in northern Vojvodina, around Subotica and Senta. The area belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary until 1918, and after the borders were drawn by the 1920 Treaty of Trianon, a large number of Hungarians remained within the newly founded Yugoslavia. Today Hungarian is one of the official languages of Vojvodina, with Hungarian-language schools and media, but its share continues to fall because of emigration and population aging.

ranking.name: Bosnian
ranking.description: Bosnian is the language of the Bosniak Muslims of the southwestern Sandžak region; it is almost mutually intelligible with Serbian but retains more Turkish loanwords from the Ottoman period. After the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, the Bosniaks formally named their language Bosnian to stress their national identity, and it now enjoys local official status in cities such as Novi Pazar.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: The ancestors of the Roma originated in northern India and entered the Balkan Peninsula through the Byzantine Empire sometime before the 14th century, so Romani preserves vocabulary close to Hindi. The Roma community in Serbia is in fact larger than the census figures show, because many registered as Serbs or switched to speaking Serbian, and they have long faced poverty and inadequate education; Romani is mostly passed down only within the family.

language.history: Serbian belongs to the South Slavic branch, and in the Middle Ages religious and legal texts were written in Old Church Slavonic. In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić reformed the Cyrillic alphabet and built a standard language on popular spoken usage, so that each letter corresponds to one sound. In the Yugoslav period Serbo-Croatian was officially promoted and the Latin alphabet also became increasingly widespread; after the state broke up in the 1990s, Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Montenegro each named their language separately. The 2006 constitution designated Cyrillic as the official script, but in daily life both alphabets are used.

ranking.name: Pljeskavica (Serbian hamburger patty)
ranking.description: A large patty of mixed ground pork, beef, lamb and other meats seasoned with onion, grilled over charcoal and served in a flatbread called lepinja, with kajmak cream, ajvar red pepper relish and raw onion.
ranking.history: The technique of charcoal-grilling ground meat comes from the Ottoman grilling culture; during the several centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, grilled-meat traditions were left throughout the region. Leskovac in southern Serbia is famous for charcoal grilling, and from the 20th century this large patty spread from there across the country to become the most popular street fast food. Leskovac holds a grill festival every late summer that includes attempts to make giant pljeskavice and draws large crowds of visitors; in Serbia its status is like that of the hamburger in the United States.

ranking.name: Ćevapi
ranking.description: Finger-sized small sausage-shaped rolls of ground meat grilled over charcoal, usually served in portions of 5 to 10 with chopped raw onion and flatbread.
ranking.history: The name "ćevapi" derives from the Turkish "kebap" (grilled meat); it is a form of grilled meat introduced during Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia later each developed different recipes. From the 19th century the grill houses of Belgrade and Leskovac were famous for it, and in the Yugoslav period it became a national food eaten throughout the country. Serbia and Bosnia still argue over whose version is the most authentic, which shows how much weight it carries in Balkan food identity.

ranking.name: Karađorđeva šnicla (Karađorđe's schnitzel)
ranking.description: Veal or pork cutlets rolled around kajmak cream, breaded and fried into a long cylinder, served with tartar sauce and roast potatoes.
ranking.history: This dish is generally believed to have been created in the 1950s by the Belgrade chef Mile Stojanović, reportedly inspired by chicken Kiev, but with the distinctively Serbian kajmak cream used as the filling. The name commemorates Karađorđe, who led the First Serbian Uprising against the Ottoman Empire in 1804 and was the founder of the Karađorđević dynasty. Because its appearance and taste are so appealing, people jokingly call it the "maiden's dream," and it is a classic on Serbian restaurant menus.

ranking.name: Ajvar
ranking.description: Red bell peppers are roasted until charred and peeled, then slowly simmered with garlic and vegetable oil into a thick relish, sometimes with eggplant added; it is spread on bread or served with grilled meat.
ranking.history: Chili peppers originated in the Americas and reached the Balkans in the 16th–17th centuries through the Ottoman trade network, becoming an important local crop. The name "ajvar" comes from the Turkish "havyar" (caviar): in the 19th century Belgrade sold large amounts of Danube caviar, and when caviar later became scarce and expensive, the red pepper relish was nicknamed "red caviar" and kept the name. Every autumn, when bell peppers are in abundant supply, Serbian families roast peppers and cook the relish together in their yards, then jar it to keep through the winter, making it an important seasonal family activity.

ranking.name: Gibanica
ranking.description: A savory pie baked from layers of thin phyllo pastry filled with white cheese and beaten egg, crisp outside and moist inside, often eaten with yogurt for breakfast.
ranking.history: The thin-pastry technique was inherited from the Byzantine and Ottoman pastry traditions, and the name is generally thought to come from the Serbian "gibati" (to fold, to sway), referring to the way the dough is folded in layers. Gibanica is an indispensable food at Serbian family celebrations; it appears at Christmas, at Easter, and at the family patron saint's day, the slava, which was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2014. At Christmas some families hide a coin in the pie, and whoever finds it will symbolically have good luck in the new year.
